summary: Updates the conceptual sending algorithm in RFC 2461 so that an IPv6 host can share traffic among equivalent routers for different destinations. The original algorithm did not do load sharing and suggested schemes that were problematic in practice. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo updates how an IPv6 host chooses among equally suitable routers. It recommends using a hash that includes the destination address so traffic to different destinations can be spread across routers.

how does an ipv6 host choose between multiple routers

how does ipv6 choose between equivalent routers
how does ipv6 router load sharing work
subtitle: A hash-based method for sharing IPv6 traffic across equivalent routers.

tldr.problem: The IPv6 sending algorithm did not specify load sharing when multiple routers were equally suitable, and simple tie-breaking could cause problems.
tldr.mechanism: A host that distributes traffic among equivalent routers SHOULD use a hash-based choice that considers at least the destination address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4311 updates RFC 2461, giving hosts a way to share load while keeping a destination's traffic on a stable router.

today: RFC 4311 is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 2461. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes RFC 4311.

sections.title: Choosing Among Equivalent Routers
sections.content:
When a host has no destination-cache entry for an off-link destination, or its current router is unreachable, it chooses a next hop. Sometimes multiple routers are equivalent, leaving the host to break a tie. Always choosing one router does not share load, while simple round-robin or random choices can make paths unstable or hard to diagnose.

Load sharing can also be undesirable when one router has enough capacity and predictable traffic paths are useful for troubleshooting.
sections.plainLanguage: A host may have more than one suitable router for a destination. A simple choice can send too much traffic through one router or make paths harder to predict.

sections.title: Hashing the Destination to Select a Router
sections.content:
When a host chooses among multiple equivalent routers, it SHOULD support a method that distributes traffic for different destinations rather than always choosing the same router. If it performs load sharing, it SHOULD use a hash-based scheme that takes at least the destination IP address into account. The memo does not say whether load sharing should be enabled by default.

While a destination-cache entry exists, traffic for that destination uses the same router. With a hash-based choice, the same destination continues to use the same router after the cache entry is deleted, as long as the equivalent-router list is unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: The host can use a calculation based on the destination to choose a router. That keeps one destination on the same router while allowing other destinations to use different routers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: If router selection is predictable, an application may create traffic that all hashes to one router, causing a denial-of-service attack against that router. A less predictable hash makes this harder. A malicious local application can bypass the algorithm for its own traffic, and remote attackers can still overload routers directly; the RFC says this method has no significant incremental effect on Internet infrastructure security.
sections.plainLanguage: Predictable choices can let an attacker direct many flows to one router. A less predictable hash makes that harder, but cannot prevent all ways to overload a router.
